transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Well, thank you for seeing me. I suppose what brings me in is... I keep hearing these very clear voices. Mostly in my apartment, but also sometimes when I'm at the museum. I go to the art museum on Tuesdays because it's free for seniors, and it's usually so quiet in the photography wing. I used to do a lot of photography myself, back when film was still the standard. I had this beautiful darkroom setup in my basement before I moved to the apartment. I miss the smell of the chemicals, actually. But anyway, the voices... it sounds like women whispering, right from behind the walls. They tell me which photographs belong in the archive. It's very specific. They have strong opinions on composition, which is interesting because my mother was always very critical of my framing when I took family portraits. She never liked how I cut off the top of my uncle's hat in that one picture from 1982.
How long have you been hearing these voices—days, weeks, or longer?

Oh, it's been much longer than a few weeks. I'd say about eight months now. Eight months of the voices, and that's also when I became absolutely certain that people are watching my archive. Eight months ago... that would have been right around October. I remember because the neighborhood kids were so loud, running across my lawn in their little costumes. They completely trampled my hydrangeas. I spent three years getting the soil acidity just right so they'd bloom that perfect shade of blue. You have to use aluminum sulfate, you know, but you have to be so careful because if you use too much, it just burns the roots right up. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she swore by coffee grounds, but her bushes always looked a bit sickly to me, just sort of limp. She moved to Florida shortly after that, actually. Sarasota, I think, or maybe Naples. Her daughter lived down there. But yes, it's been about eight months since the whispering and the watching started.
Over these past eight months, have you noticed any changes in your ability to manage daily tasks, work, or relationships because of these experiences?

Well, yes, things have gotten... difficult. I used to be on the board for the local historical society, you know. I haven't been to a meeting in... oh, I don't even know how long. I completely lost the trust of everyone there. They wanted to digitize everything, which I suppose makes sense, but I was so focused on the physical archive because of what the voices were telling me. I missed the meetings, and then I started missing my bills. My cousin, Arthur, he had to step in. Arthur is a very practical man. He used to be an accountant for a firm downtown before they got bought out by one of those massive conglomerates. He always wore these incredibly loud ties—paisley, mostly, sometimes stripes—which you wouldn't expect from an accountant. He said it was his one rebellion. Anyway, Arthur had to take over my finances because I just couldn't keep track of the money anymore. And then there was an incident at the museum... one of the administrators actually had to intervene because I wasn't safe managing public events on my own anymore. I was supposed to be giving a talk on early 20th-century portraiture, and I just... couldn't do it. The administrator, a lovely woman named Sarah, she always wears these beautiful silk scarves. I asked her where she got them once, and she said she finds them at estate sales. I used to love estate sales. You can find the most remarkable silver serving pieces if you get there early enough on a Saturday morning. But yes, Arthur and Sarah have been doing so much for me because I just can't manage the appointments or anything else right now.

Besides the voices and worries about being watched, have you noticed yourself feeling less interested in things you used to enjoy, having less energy to start activities, or feeling emotionally flat or withdrawn from people?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been feeling rather... flat. There are these long stretches now where I just sit at my kitchen table. I have these little herb pots on the windowsill—basil, thyme, a bit of rosemary—and I just watch them dry out. I used to be so meticulous about watering them. You really have to be careful with basil, it wilts so dramatically if you miss even one day, but then it perks right back up when you give it a drink. It’s almost theatrical, really. My friend Eleanor used to say her basil plants were the biggest drama queens in her garden. Eleanor has this magnificent garden, or she did, anyway. She used to invite me over for tea on her patio, and lately... I just don't call her back. Or anyone, really. Even when they invite me to a gallery opening or a concert, I just can't find the interest. I used to love the symphony. The cello section always gave me goosebumps. My grandfather played the cello, actually. He had this gorgeous instrument, made in Germany in the late 1800s. The wood was so dark and rich. He used to practice in the parlor, and the sound would just fill the whole house. But now, even thinking about going out to hear music... it just feels like too much effort, and I don't really feel anything about missing it.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports over 8 months of persistent auditory hallucinations (whispering female voices commenting on and directing his archival activities) and a fixed persecutory/referential delusion that people are watching his archive. These positive symptoms co-occur with prominent negative symptoms—flat affect, anhedonia, social withdrawal, and avolition (neglecting plants, declining social invitations, no longer enjoying music). There is clear functional decline across multiple domains: loss of board position, financial mismanagement requiring a relative to intervene, and inability to perform professional duties at the museum. No manic or depressive mood episode of sufficient duration or severity is described to account for the psychotic symptoms, and the hallucinations are not confined to mood-episode periods, making a schizoaffective or mood-disorder-with-psychotic-features diagnosis less likely. The presence of hallucinations (not just delusions) rules against delusional disorder. Duration exceeds 6 months, satisfying chronicity criteria for schizophrenia, and no specific subtype (paranoid, catatonic, etc.) is clearly predominant, supporting the unspecified subtype code.
